Would absolutely invade my neighbor again. I bought Total War: Warhammer III expecting a fantasy strategy game. Instead, I got a comprehensive political education where every faction has apparently discovered a different way to violate international law.

Kislev: Your economy is collapsing, your cities are freezing, and everyone is angry.
Solution? Conscription. You are now running Eastern Europe Simulator.

Cathay: The emperor has centralized everything, controls trade, maintains an enormous bureaucracy, and occasionally turns into a dragon.

Khorne: Diplomacy is for cowards. Their policy consists of: Find country. Kill country. Kill the survivors. Ask why nobody wants diplomatic relations. Somehow still has better economic growth than my country.

Nurgle: You don't conquer territory. You improve public health outcomes negatively. The game should honestly have a warning: “Playing as Nurgle may violate several international conventions.”

Slaanesh: Everything is about excess. Gold? Excess. Food? Excess. War crimes? Excess. This faction somehow made the Geneva Convention feel like a suggestion box.

Tzeentch: Every time I think I understand what is happening, Tzeentch changes the rules. I don't even play the faction anymore. I just assume my government has been overthrown by my own advisor.

Skaven: Fascism? Democracy? Communism? No. Rat Communism. Everyone is equal because everyone is equally disposable. The Skaven have successfully invented a political system where the state owns everything, the workers own nothing, and the leadership owns several million slaves. Karl Marx would uninstall this.

Greenskins: No ideology. No manifesto. No political platform. Just Boiz doing WAAAGH. Honestly, the most honest political movement in the game.

Chaos Dwarfs: Basically, industrial capitalism entering the chat. They looked at slavery, child labor, pollution, weapons manufacturing, and environmental destruction and said: “What if we made this an economic strategy?” And somehow it works.

Vampire Counts: Immigration policy is simple. Everyone comes in. Nobody leaves. The ultimate closed-border policy.

Empire: A technologically advanced bureaucracy held together by paperwork, artillery, religious disputes, and one guy named Karl Franz desperately trying to prevent the entire country from collapsing. So... government simulator.

Dwarfs: They have spent 2,000 years maintaining a spreadsheet of everyone who has ever mildly inconvenienced them. Honestly, terrifying administrative efficiency.

Wood Elves: “Protect nature.” Burns down your settlement because it is located slightly too close to a tree. Environmentalism has never been this aggressive.

This is an excellent game. It teaches economics, diplomacy, logistics, military strategy, religion, political extremism, industrialization, colonialism, environmental policy, and why giving one person absolute power is probably a bad idea.

10/10. Apparently you are not supposed to call exterminating an entire species “population management.”

A Great Total War Game Held Back by DLC and Multiplayer Issues

Total War: Warhammer III has a vast campaign and an incredibly vibrant unit roster. The faction mechanics are generally fun and creative, and learning how to use each faction’s unique mechanics can make campaigns much easier. However, these mechanics are not necessarily what makes you overpowered—you still need to play it like a Total War game: build your economy, develop your settlements, raise more armies, and conquer your enemies.

Unfortunately, the biggest problem with the game is the DLC model.

To be honest, a lot of the fun feels locked behind DLC. Without the DLCs, many factions have only partial unit rosters, which makes the base game feel significantly less complete. The amount of content available behind the paywall can be frustrating, especially when you consider how much of the game's appeal comes from its enormous variety of units.

Personally, I think it would have been much better if the developers focused more on faction DLCs rather than splitting individual units and additional content across numerous DLCs. The game already has an incredible foundation; making the core rosters feel more complete would make the experience much more satisfying.

The second major issue is multiplayer.

The multiplayer ladder is currently buggy, and the matchmaking system feels poorly designed for a competitive game. At the moment, two players enter a lobby and then choose their factions. The problem is that players can leave during the army-building stage without any meaningful consequences. This means that if someone sees a matchup they don't like, they can simply quit and search for another opponent.

I think a better competitive system would be:

Players choose their factions before matchmaking.
They are then matched with an opponent based on those faction choices.
Leaving the lobby after being matched should result in an ELO penalty/loss.
Army building should have a fixed time limit, such as 2 minutes.

I got into Total War: Warhammer III quite by chance. Even though I love tactical, turn-based, and strategy games, I was initially very hesitant to try this one. The turning point came when my friends started streaming it for me. They eventually talked me into buying it, and... it completely hooked me. I started enjoying it so much that I decided to hunt down all the achievements (including the notoriously hard ones, like winning a battle with a 10-to-1 disadvantage) and explore almost everything the game has to offer. Here are my thoughts after hundreds of hours of playtime.

The Positives:
First and foremost, I have to praise the visuals. The game features beautiful graphics and a massive, brilliantly designed map, especially in the Immortal Empires mode. I was also pleasantly surprised by how deep and interesting the lore is, considering the Warhammer universe was completely off my radar before.

The biggest draw, however, is the gameplay and replayability. The game offers a massive variety of mechanics, and thanks to the dynamic decisions made by the AI, no two campaigns ever unfold the same way. A huge plus is how distinct the factions are. Playing as Grand Cathay, for example, is a completely different experience from spreading your influence as the Skaven with Clan Eshin or Clan Moulder. Each faction has its own specific mechanics, which keeps the game constantly fresh.

The Negatives:
Unfortunately, the game has its dark sides, the most prominent being the pricing policy. The base game itself is quite expensive, but the real issue is the sheer amount of content locked behind paid DLCs. Sure, you can play without them, but you miss out on a lot of tactical options and legendary lords, which is quite off-putting and taints the overall experience.

Another disappointing aspect is the technical state of the multiplayer. More than once, my friends and I encountered minor bugs or complete game crashes, which can be incredibly frustrating right in the middle of a tense battle.

Conclusion:
If it weren't for the massive amount of expensive paid content, this would be an absolutely stellar game. I definitely don't want to say it's a bad game – on the contrary, it's an exceptionally high-quality strategy title that can keep you glued to your screen for a very long time. It's just a huge shame that so much of its true potential is locked behind extra paywalls.

As someone approaching the close to 1000 hr mark on the franchise (WH1-3) let me give an honest review.

Firstly lets start with the elephant in the room all the bad reviews point out... Yes, there are a lot of DLCs for the game. Yes, you need to own older versions for some of them. Do you need them to have fun? Absolutely not. You can own every DLC in this game (like I do) and I promise you well still end up spending hours and hours on the same couple of factions you find out you like the most, and still never play the same campaign exactly the same way. Even with just the base game factions. You make your decisions every campaign, the game might have good vs evil or separate chaos corruption based "guidelines" for you to make your campaign easier, but there's nothing saying you cant go against the grain and make enemies of all those factions that would typically deem you friends, or maybe you want to do a campaign with only 1 unit type. The countless hours you can spend replaying the same lord and having a different experience each time is amazing.

Now with that being said, should you pay full price? No, absolutely not. The game goes on sale often, as well as the DLCs. Pick it up at a bargain, id say even 25 dollars is a steal for this game. If you have a faction in mind that you really like the look of and think it will be fun, grab that too. 

How are the DLCs? Well, your always going to have ups and downs when it comes to what a DLC provides, especially if you like to play the game a certain way. Are all the DLCs fantastic? As someone who owns every single one, and has played them all, I can whole heartedly tell you...No. They arent all fantastic. Does that mean they arent fun? No. I have never played a DLC in this entire franchise that I couldnt have fun with. I find myself returning to DLCs that I didnt care for as much as others even after 4, 5, 6 playthroughs. For example, I dont much care for the wood elves faction, some people love them, they arent my favorite. But I have still played each mulitple times. 

So which DLCs do I recommend for new players? (Without buying any of the older games) Anything that looks cool! The hardest faction to play in this game  in my opinion for a new player is going to be the chaos dwarves. They have an economy system that is quite unique and takes a bit of getting used to, however the trade off there is their military battles are usually quite easy. My personal top picks if your just starting out and absolutely must have a DLC instead of just the base game would be  The prophet and the warlock DLC, Bashiva character pack for cathay, The Omens of destruction and Thrones of decay DLCs both of these are fantastic to buy in the whole pack because they are loaded with strong, fun, relatively easy to play lords. 

My recommendation would be to give this game a good honest try. Its loads of fun, has pretty good graphics, and if you really want to have fun, go into a skirmish Vs Ai battle or play with a friend and spectate, and just throw your troops into the enemies, Press K to enter cinematic mode, and watch the battle, see if that doesnt immediately make your experience 100x better. 

Final Notes: If youve made it this far, thank you for reading my book of a review, I usually dont review many games and when i do its short and to the point, but I feel this one deserves a longer one. Plus, have you noticed at the time of most of these negative reviews are after only just a couple hours of playing the game, and then the people who complain still manage to rack up another 20, 30, even 40 more hours? When you look at the store page, it’s understandable to have a minor cortisol spike. There's three mainline games and a decade worth of Lord Packs, seeing "90% of the game's content behind a paywall" turns a lot of people off.

Here is the truth: You don't need to buy the extra content to get hundreds of hours of fun.

1. The base game is already packed

You don’t need 40 DLCs to enjoy the core experience. Simply buying Warhammer 3 unlocks the massive Immortal Empires map alongside a stacked cast of base factions: Grand Cathay, Kislev, all four Chaos Gods (Skarbrand, N'Kari, Ku'gath, Kairos), a fully customizable Daemon Prince, and even Be'lakor representing the Warriors of Chaos. That alone gives you hundreds of hours of content before you even think about opening your wallet again.

2. DLCs are modular, not mandatory

This isn't a pay-to-win live-service game where you get locked out of the fun if you don't buy the latest pass. All the DLC factions, lords, and units still appear on the campaign map as AI opponents for you to fight for free. You only pay if you specifically look at a faction and go: "Yeah, I want to personally control that exact Character." If you don't care about playing a specific Lord or accessing niche unit rosters, you are losing basically nothing other than a few unique mechanics and quirks. 

3. Credit where it's due

Creative Assembly built something truly incredible here. Gathering three massive games worth of map, lore, and mechanics into one seamless sandbox is a major achievement. The scale is staggering, the flavour is unmatched, and at no point during a standard campaign does the game aggressively force you to buy extra stuff. It’s just sitting there on the shelf should you fall in love with the game and eventually want additional flavour.

Verdict:

Buy the base game. Play Miao Ying, Katarin, or Skarbrand. Unify your realm (or burn it down). If you put 100 hours into it and decide you want to play as a mutated rat with radioactive gatling guns or as a crazed ginger scottish OSHA violation, grab that specific DLC on a sale. If not, enjoy one of the best strategy games ever made without spending a single extra penny.

10/10 — Glare at the DLC list, ignore it and withhold judgement then go conquer the world.

Yet even so the game (and all in the series) is absolutely brilliant. One of the awesome parts is that they followed through with their promise of three games, each with a multitude of DLCs, that all contribute their content to any later game in the series. So while each game provided 4-5 factions at start, acquiring all the content provides more than a hundred. Some ppl hate DLCs, that attitude is misplaced here. They aren't cut content, rather content that would never have been made without the DLC structure. Even so the game is still very much playable without a single DLC or older game in the series, getting a full experience. Even tho I love them, for some the DLCs are a big drawback.

The game is severely moddable.
